meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Is That a Gun in Your Pocket, or Are You Just Glad to See Me?'?
meta.ogDescription: It is Mae West's line — but not from her 1930s films. Earliest evidence: a 1958 book recalling a 1944 stage ad-lib about a sword.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The line really is hers — just not from the film everyone names. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no rival claimant and concludes the joke family originated with West, but its earliest located evidence is a 1958 book recalling a 1944 Broadway ad-lib in which the object was a sword, and the famous “gun in your pocket” wording is first printed — with no citation attached — in a 1967 compilation of her sayings. West speaks it on screen only in Sextette (1978).

source.excerpt:
Barry, playing Lieutenant Bunin, was unaccustomed to carrying a sword, and in the second act, during an embrace, his scabbard came between him and his Empress.

A covert smile stole over Mae’s face. “Lieutenant,” she ad-libbed with a Westian leer, “is that your sword or are you just glad to see me?”
trail: The earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗ is Art Cohn’s 1958 biography of producer Michael Todd, which describes West ad-libbing the joke on stage in 1944 — with a sword, not a gun.
The film everyone names is ruled out. Quote Investigator quotes Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations: the line “does not appear in that or any of her other pre-1967 movies” (QI ↗).

The famous wording first appears in The Wit and Wisdom of Mae West ↗, the 1967 G. P. Putnam’s Sons compilation edited by Joseph Weintraub; Quote Investigator ↗ found it on page 59 with no citation attached.
West finally says it on screen in Sextette (1978) — directed by Ken Hughes ↗, screenplay by Herbert Baker from West’s own play. Wikiquote ↗ lists that film as the sourced home of the line.
source.cutTag: Art Cohn, The Nine Lives of Michael Todd (1958), p. 193
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator ↗, and note what it is not: the object is a sword, the setting is a Broadway stage, and the telling is second-hand, published in 1958 about a 1944 performance. The scene checks out — Gene Barry’s filmography ↗ records him as Lieutenant Bunin in Catherine Was Great, the play West wrote and starred in, which opened at the Shubert Theatre on 2 August 1944 ↗ under Mike Todd’s production.

author.name: Mae West
author.heading: Mae West
author.bio: Mae West wrote her own material before she was famous for delivering it — Wikipedia ↗ describes her as an actress, singer, comedian, screenwriter and playwright who began writing her own risqué plays and frequently wrote her own film dialogue. That authorship is why a quip with no traceable script line still lands on her: she was the plausible source of anything sharp said in her voice. She wrote and starred in the 1944 Broadway show Catherine Was Great, and her final film, Sextette (1978), was based on a script she had written in 1959.

Joseph Weintraub (New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1967), 59, and is spoken by West in Sextette, dir. Ken Hughes (1978).

misattribution.heading: Where the story goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Almost nobody misattributes this line to the wrong person. They misattribute it to the wrong place — and that is the part worth fixing.

items.who: She Done Him Wrong (1933), or any of her 1930s films
items.why: The single most repeated claim about this line, and it is refuted by the standard reference. Quote Investigator ↗ quotes Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations: the line “does not appear in that or any of her other pre-1967 movies.” Oxford University Press makes the same point — it “did not occur in a film until the 1978 Sextette” (OUP ↗).

There is no settled wording. The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations ↗ gives “pleased to see me”; Wikiquote ↗ renders the Sextette line “happy to see me”; and the earliest documented form has a sword, not a gun at all.

Quote Investigator ↗ prints a passage from Lysistrata in which a magistrate accuses a herald of hiding a lance under his cloak, and presents it explicitly as “a precursor to this expression” — the same comic mechanism, not a source for these words.

West told Films and Filming that she said it to an officer welcoming her back to Hollywood, and Jill Watts’s 2001 biography dates that meeting to her 1936 arrival (Barry Popik ↗). Quote Investigator ↗ notes the claim was published decades afterwards, in the 1980s.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-supported account: the joke is Mae West’s, but the earliest evidence for it is a 1958 book recalling a 1944 Broadway ad-lib about a sword, and the famous “gun in your pocket” wording reaches print in 1967 with no citation attached — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting mis-sourced
lead: This is the textbook case of a line that belongs to a star but not to the movie everyone names. Because Mae West wrote so much of her own material, a quip in her voice feels like it must have a scene attached — and audiences supplied one. The usual candidate is She Done Him Wrong (1933). Quote Investigator ↗ quotes Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations flatly: the line “does not appear in that or any of her other pre-1967 movies.”

The paper trail runs the other way round from the legend. The joke shows up first in print as a piece of theatre gossip, drifts through novels with the object swapped out, gets collected into a book of West’s sayings without a source, and only then arrives on film — in 1978, with West herself finally saying it out loud to a gangster.
context.detailsSummary: The object keeps changing: sword, pipe, gun, rod, pencil, banana
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology tracks the swap. The 1958 telling has a sword; a 1961 novel by Robert Switzer has a pipe; Roderick Thorp’s The Detective (1966) has a gun and credits West; Andrew Sarris in 1968 has “packin’ a rod”; a 1982 Boston Globe piece has a radio DJ using a pencil; and by 1989 a New York newspaper is treating the banana version as the well-worn one. See the full chronology at Quote Investigator ↗.

The verb wanders too. Quote Investigator transcribes the Sextette line as “glad to see me”; Wikiquote ↗ renders the same film’s line as “happy to see me”; and the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations ↗ gives “pleased to see me.” There is no single settled wording.
context.pull: The famous version reached the screen last, not first.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located evidence is Art Cohn's The Nine Lives of Michael Todd (Random House, 1958), quote page 193, reporting Mae West's 1944 ad-lib to Gene Barry as "Lieutenant, is that your sword or are you just glad to see me?"; the wording "Is that a gun in your pocket, or are you just glad to see me?" first appears in The Wit and Wisdom of Mae West (1967), page 59, with no citation; West delivers it in the 1978 film Sextette to George Hamilton (Vance Norton); the Yale Book of Quotations states the line does not appear in She Done Him Wrong or any of her other pre-1967 movies; a Lysistrata passage is presented as a precursor; West's own 1930s policeman claim was published in Films and Filming in 1983; QI concludes the joke family originated with Mae West and finds no support for rival claimants.

Wikiquote lists "Is that a gun in your pocket, or are you just happy to see me?" in its main sourced Quotes section, attributed to Sextette (1978), citing Quote Investigator and the Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations; it gives Mae West's dates as 17 August 1893 to 22 November 1980.

Barry Popik's entry credits the saying to Mae West, states the saying was not in her movies and that She Done Him Wrong is frequently and incorrectly cited, and quotes Jill Watts's Mae West: An Icon in Black and White (2001) placing the origin at West's 1936 arrival in Los Angeles greeting an LAPD officer.

Oxford University Press's misquotation post states the line "did not occur in a film until the 1978 Sextette" and gives the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations form as "Is that a gun in your pocket, or are you just pleased to see me?"

Wikipedia gives Mae West's dates as August 17, 1893 – November 22, 1980, describes her as an actress, singer, comedian, screenwriter and playwright who wrote her own plays and film dialogue, states she wrote and played the title role in Catherine Was Great (1944) produced by Mike Todd, and that Sextette (1978) was her final film, based on a script she had written in 1959.
Wikipedia states Sextette (1978) was directed by Ken Hughes with a screenplay by Herbert Baker based on Mae West's play of the same title, and that George Hamilton played the gangster Vance Norton.
Wikipedia's Gene Barry article lists him as Lieutenant Bunin in Catherine Was Great (1944); his dates are 1919–2009.
Wikipedia states Catherine Was Great was written by and starred Mae West, was produced by Mike Todd, and opened at the Shubert Theatre on August 2, 1944.
